To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
CCN3, an endogenous protein with anti inflammatory and anti nociceptive properties, regulates MMP9 expression in response to inflammatory pain.
i) CCN3 is downregulated during the induction of inflammation ii) CCN3 inhibits MMP9 and iii) CCN3 regulates MMP9 and MMP9 expression during inflammation.

i) the expression and secretion of CCN3 is down regulated in the spinal cord of animals with neuropathic pain ii) CCN3 regulates the expression of two MMPs, MMP9 and 2, which in turn regulate the expression of the nociceptive receptor TRPV1.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the role of the protein CCN3 in inflammation and pain.
the role of the protein CCN3 in pain.
the identification of the molecular mechanisms that underlie neuropathic pain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the data presented by Kular et al., 2012, are suggestive of a potential role for CCN 3 in the regulation MMP2 and MMP 9, and that this potential role may be involved in inflammatory pain.
CCN3 may be involved in pain regulation via the regulation of MMP2 and MMP 9.
CCN3 is a potential regulator of pain and that its role in this process is likely to be complex and multifaceted.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CCN3 is a pain killer.
the CCN3 protein is a potential target for the treatment of pain and that it is a good candidate for future studies in this field.
CCN3 has been demonstrated to be a negative regulator of MMPs in the spinal cord and DRG, and that this is one of the mechanisms by which CCN3 may regulate the pain process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CCN3 can modulate the activity of MMP2 and MMP 9, and that this effect is mediated by the modulation of the activity of ERK1/2 and p38MAPK.
the expression of a CCN3 is reduced following inflammation, and this is accompanied by the upregulation of two MMPs.
